clue.text: Detective has to stick to Oxford, perhaps

parts.note: to stick is to gum, as with glue
an Oxford is a style of lace-up shoe, so this is an example of footwear

explanation.surface: A detective is obliged to stay loyal to Oxford, the city or the university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oxford' looks like the city or the university, but here it is a kind of lace-up footwear.
explanation.definitionFit: Gumshoe is old American slang for a private investigator, from the soft-soled shoes worn for quiet tailing.

clue.text: Less willing to work after completion of building, workman. .

indicators.note: the lazier piece comes after the letter from building
the completion of a word is its final letter

parts.note: someone less willing to work is lazier

explanation.surface: Once the building is done, a workman becomes idler.
explanation.definitionFit: A glazier is a tradesman who fits glass into windows.

clue.text: … worked with more than rudimentary gumption

indicators.note: worked letters are kneaded into a new shape
a rudiment is a first step, so only the first letter of than is used

explanation.surface: Continuing the workman: he laboured with more than basic common sense.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis continues 1 Down. 'worked' rearranges WITH, MORE and T, the rudimentary start of 'than'.
explanation.definitionFit: Native common sense or shrewdness is called mother wit, much as gumption means practical sense.

clue.text: Drove to store, by the sound of it

indicators.note: the word is judged by how it is pronounced, not spelt

parts.note: a hoard is a hidden store

explanation.surface: Someone drove to the shop, or so it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drove' looks like the verb of driving to a shop; it is a noun, a herd or crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: A drove is a large moving crowd or herd, as is a horde.

clue.text: For a walk East European goes round the mountains, climbing

indicators.note: in a down clue climbing means the letters go upwards, read in reverse
one word encircles the other

parts.note: a Dane is a European
the Alps are the mountains of Europe

explanation.surface: A man from eastern Europe takes a hike around the mountains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'climbing' turns E + DAN(ALPS)E upwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A seafront promenade, a place laid out for strolling, is an esplanade.

clue.text: Gilbert was injured, and spoke incoherently

parts.note: W. S. Gilbert signed his comic verse 'Bab', as in the Bab Ballads
someone who was injured may have bled

explanation.surface: Gilbert got hurt and could only mumble nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: W. S. Gilbert, librettist of the Gilbert and Sullivan operettas, published his comic verse as the Bab Ballads under the pen name Bab.
explanation.definitionFit: To babble is to talk rapidly and without making sense, so the past tense fits speaking incoherently.

clue.text: Progress, in some degree, for a zealot

indicators.note: one word sits inside the other

parts.note: a bit is some degree, as in a bit tired
to progress is to go

explanation.surface: Some advancement, to a small extent, for a fanatic.
explanation.definitionFit: A bigot is an intolerant person fixed on their views, close to a fanatic.

clue.text: Date of Derby in doubt

indicators.note: doubt suggests things are unsettled, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The date of the Derby horse race is uncertain.
explanation.walkthrough: The Derby is a famous English horse race; 'Date' seems to be its calendar date but is a romantic partner.
explanation.definitionFit: A date can mean the person one is going out with romantically, such as a male partner.

clue.text: Inclined to sound fast

indicators.note: sound here means the word is heard, not seen

parts.note: Lent is the Christian period of fasting

explanation.surface: Someone tended to sound rushed.
explanation.definitionFit: To have leant is to have tilted or tended, both senses of inclined.

clue.text: Landing-craft leaves Wales on the way up to Edinburgh, perhaps

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece sits on top of the other
one letter leaves, so it is removed

parts.note: the DUKW was a Second World War amphibious landing vehicle
W is the abbreviation for Wales

indicators.note: in a down clue going up means reading backwards

parts.note: a mode is a way of doing something

explanation.surface: A landing craft departs Wales, heading north to Edinburgh.
explanation.walkthrough: The DUKW, known as a 'duck', loses W for Wales. 'Edinburgh' looks like a destination but is a duke's title.
explanation.definitionFit: The Duke of Edinburgh's title is an example of a ducal rank or territory.

clue.text: I was tired, to some extent, being out of bed

indicators.note: only part of the words is used, so the letters sit inside the phrase was tired

explanation.surface: Someone admits to being a bit weary on getting up.
explanation.definitionFit: Astir means up and moving about, as someone is after rising in the morning.

clue.text: The way to carry bacon?

parts.note: bacon comes from a pig, so it travels on a pig's back, a punning name for a ride carried on someone's shoulders

explanation.definitionFit: A piggyback is a ride on another's back, and the pun takes it literally as bacon riding on the pig.

clue.text: Crude, but in a gentle fashion

indicators.note: to fashion something is to shape it anew, so the letters of in a gentle are remade

explanation.surface: Something is called rough, though delivered in a soft and kindly way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fashion' reads as a noun, 'in a gentle fashion', but it is a verb telling you to rework IN A GENTLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Crude and inelegant both describe something rough and lacking refinement or grace.

clue.text: The artist Edward valued

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, the usual crossword artist
Ted is a short form of the name Edward

explanation.surface: An artist named Edward is held in high regard.
explanation.definitionFit: To be rated is to be assessed or esteemed, much as something valued is.

clue.text: Went in a boat or in a car, would you say?

indicators.note: the question asks how the word is pronounced, signalling a word that sounds the same

parts.note: travelling in a car is to ride, past tense rode

explanation.surface: A question about whether someone travelled by boat or by car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'would you say?' tells you the car journey word, RODE, is heard, giving the same sound spelt the boating way.
explanation.definitionFit: Rowing is propelling a boat with oars, so having rowed is having gone by boat.

clue.text: Sported in storm, it keeps the rain off

indicators.note: a storm throws things about, so the letters are tossed into a new order

explanation.surface: Worn during bad weather, a garment shields you from rain.
explanation.definitionFit: A projecting moulding above a window or door, throwing off rainwater, is called a dripstone.

clue.text: 'ibernating animal has to stop in city

parts.note: a hamster hibernates; the dropped H of 'ibernating says to drop the H of hamster too
a dam stops the flow of water

explanation.surface: A sleepy pet rodent must stay put in town, in a Cockney accent.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in ''ibernating' copies the Cockney dropped H, so the hibernating animal, a hamster, also loses its H.
explanation.definitionFit: Amsterdam is the capital city of the Netherlands.

clue.text: A triangle put on top of another figure

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits above the second

parts.note: to put is to set
a square is a geometric figure, like a triangle

explanation.surface: A triangle is placed above some other shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A set square is a triangular drawing instrument used for right angles.

clue.text: Cannibalism, with no holds barred

explanation.surface: Cannibalism is a no-holds-barred affair.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally dogs eating their own kind, the phrase also describes ruthless competition where anything goes.

clue.text: Harm returning ruler in colourful surroundings? Not I!

indicators.note: something returning goes back, so the assembled letters are read in reverse
the ruler is placed inside the colourful word, which surrounds it
Not I says to leave out the letter I

parts.note: colourful things are tinted
an emir is a Muslim ruler

explanation.surface: A ruler comes home amid bright decoration, and someone insists they caused no harm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not I!' drops I from TINTED to give TNTED; EMIR goes 'in' it as TNEMIRTED, and 'returning' turns the whole lot round. 'surroundings' only reinforces the containment.
explanation.definitionFit: Detriment is damage or loss suffered, a close synonym of hurt.

clue.text: About mechanization of clerical work; cleric is poker-faced

indicators.note: about means around, so one word goes round the other

parts.note: a dean is a senior clergyman
ADP is automatic data processing, the computerising of office work

explanation.surface: A clergyman keeps a straight face over office automation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clerical' and 'cleric' share a root but mean office work and a churchman.
explanation.definitionFit: Deadpan means expressionless, keeping a straight face.

clue.text: One, for instance, is like it

parts.note: to dig something is slang for liking it
taken as written

explanation.surface: A remark that one example happens to resemble something.
explanation.definitionFit: Numerals such as one are each a single figure, the basic unit of counting.

clue.text: In America they reverse the ending of this dramatic art

definitions.text: In America they reverse the ending of this dramatic art

parts.words: In America they reverse the ending of this dramatic art
parts.note: the British spelling of the stage art ends -re, which Americans spell -er

explanation.definitionFit: Theatre is the art of drama, spelt with -er in American English.

clue.text: The bearing shown in a warrior's shield

indicators.note: the bearing is displayed inside the other letters, so it is placed within them

parts.note: GI is an American soldier; the 's adds S
E, east, is a compass bearing

explanation.surface: A heraldic device is depicted on a fighter's shield.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bearing' suggests heraldry on the shield, but it is the compass point E.
explanation.definitionFit: The aegis was the shield of Zeus and Athena, and by extension means protection.

clue.text: Environmentalist has not smoked

explanation.surface: An eco-campaigner has never lit up.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain unsmoked bacon is called green bacon.
explanation.definitionFit: A Green is an ecology campaigner; green bacon is cured but unsmoked.

clue.text: Kill dead, accepting one pound for it

indicators.note: one word takes in the others, as a container holding them

parts.note: the late person is one who has died
I is the Roman numeral one
quid is British slang for a pound sterling

explanation.surface: A hitman is paid a single pound to finish someone off.
explanation.walkthrough: QUID is everyday British slang for a pound.
explanation.definitionFit: To liquidate a person is a euphemism for murdering them.

clue.text: Knowing there's shelter over the line

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece is placed above the other

parts.note: the lee is the sheltered side
RY, railway, is a rail line

explanation.surface: Someone shrewd finds cover above the railway.
explanation.definitionFit: Being wary or suspicious, as one who knows the risks, is being leery.

clue.text: Empty hotel without a natural base

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so the hotel surrounds the letter

parts.note: an inn is a small hotel
e is the base of natural logarithms

explanation.surface: A vacant hotel lacks any natural foundation.
explanation.definitionFit: Inane means senseless or vacuous, lacking substance.

clue.text: Remarkable people created by O. Henry (pen name)

indicators.note: the letters are made into something new, so they are reshuffled

parts.note: H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: Extraordinary characters invented by the writer O. Henry, which was itself a pseudonym.
explanation.walkthrough: O. Henry was the pen name of the American short-story writer William Sydney Porter.
explanation.definitionFit: Prodigies or marvels, people of extraordinary ability, are sometimes called phenomena.

clue.text: Check the left hand side of the hall

indicators.note: only the start of the word is kept, its right-hand part being cut off

parts.note: an auditorium is a hall for an audience

explanation.surface: Inspect the left part of the hall.
explanation.definitionFit: An audit is an official inspection of accounts, so it is a kind of checking.

clue.text: Messenger with no right of entry into New York house

indicators.note: the shortened messenger goes inside the abbreviation, entering it
a letter is removed, the messenger going without it

parts.note: a runner carries messages

explanation.surface: A courier is refused permission to enter a building in New York.
explanation.definitionFit: A convent is a religious house where nuns live together.

clue.text: Centre providing record amount of work around Sunderland

parts.note: an EP is an extended-play record
the erg is a unit of work in physics
Sunderland is in the North East of England, NE

explanation.surface: A hub providing records of how much work is done in Sunderland.
explanation.walkthrough: Sunderland is a city in North East England. 'Centre' is short for a centrepiece.
explanation.definitionFit: An epergne is an ornamental table centrepiece with dishes or holders branching from a stem.
